findings.finding: The EXCLUDE pattern `>\s*\S` also matches the stderr redirect `2>&1`, so very common commands such as `dotnet test 2>&1` or `npm test 2>&1` are never classified or trimmed.

In the default observe mode, the full raw output of every eligible Bash call is written to ~/.claude/smart-context-trimming/raw without redaction. The TTL only empties files at the next session start, so secrets can stay on disk indefinitely.

bench.ts measures reduction and lostCritical on the same hand-written FIXTURES that core.spec.ts uses to check the rules, so 0 lost and 89-91% reduction are in-sample numbers, not evidence on real logs.

When a Jev decision is accepted, applyJev rebuilds the keep-set from mandatory candidates only, so the warning groups the rules kept are dropped under errors_only. This contradicts the claim that a bad Jev decision can only make the output longer.
The live bench rests on only 3 Jev calls, so medianJevReduction 0.911 vs rule 0.894 is not a meaningful comparison.
The timeout uses Promise.race without aborting the request, so a timed-out Jev fetch keeps running, and the sleep timer is never cleared after a fast response.
The raw-save threshold uses text.length (UTF-16 chars) while planTrim uses byteLen, so multi-byte output can be trimmed with no saved raw file, or saved but never trimmed.
The 40+ hex redaction also removes git SHAs and content hashes from Jev candidates; safe but loses diagnostic context.
